text: Finance's monthly attrition report lands at 2.3% churn. The dashboard says 4.1%. Same company, same period, two very different numbers — and the first move is not to touch a single line of code.

Before changing anything, get finance's exact definition in writing: their lapse window is 180 days, not 90, and their denominator is every customer who ever enrolled, not just the ones who were ever actually at risk of churning.

Laid side by side, a longer lapse window pulls the rate down on its own, and a denominator stuffed with customers who were never real repeat buyers pulls it down even further — two reasonable definitions, never once reconciled against each other.

To confirm, the dashboard's own query gets re-run with finance's exact parameters substituted in. It lands close to 2.3% — proof the gap is fully explained by definitions, not a data error hiding somewhere.

The finding gets documented, not silently resolved in either direction: both numbers are correct under their own rules, and the dashboard keeps its original definition because it was built to answer the Sales Director's specific question.
She gets a heads-up before she hears a different number from someone else in a meeting you're not even in. Next up: a second, unrelated problem the reconciliation process itself turned up.
